fields.Front: List the seven properties of relations (the objective asks for five).
fields.Back:
1. Each relation NAME is unique in the database
2. Each CELL holds one ATOMIC value - normalized, First Normal Form (1NF)
3. Each ATTRIBUTE NAME within a table is unique
4. All values of an attribute come from the SAME DOMAIN
5. The ORDER OF ATTRIBUTES has no significance
6. Each TUPLE IS DISTINCT - no duplicate rows
7. The ORDER OF TUPLES has no significance

fields.Front: Why do the properties hold? Give the mathematical reason for tuple order, duplicates, one domain per column and atomic cells.
fields.Back: A relation is a SET, so order does not matter (property 7) and no element is repeated (property 6). The possible values at a position are determined by the DOMAIN that position is defined on (property 4). Mathematical relations are NOT necessarily normalized - Codd CHOSE relations in the relational model to be normalized (property 2), so only one value per cell.

fields.Front: Which two properties does practice sometimes bend, and how should you answer on the exam?
fields.Back: Properties 6 and 7 - no duplicates and no tuple order. In practice a query may return the same row twice, results may be displayed alphabetically, and rows may be stored on disk in an order for efficiency. 'From a theoretical standpoint, the order has no meaning' and 'you never, ever have the same row twice.' Answer exam questions from Codd's theory.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: what is wrong (if anything) with each - (a) two tables both named EMPLOYEE, (b) THINGY_TABLE with rows (Apple,Dog,77), (Orange,Cat,77), (Apple,Dog,77), (Orange,Pig,77), (c) columns YThingy, XThingy, YThingy?
fields.Back:
(a) Two relations share a NAME - property 1; 'these two tables could not exist in the same database', even if one is full-time and one part-time staff with different SSNs.
(b) Rows 1 and 3 are DUPLICATE TUPLES - property 6; 'you don't have a key that's really doing anything'.
(c) DUPLICATE ATTRIBUTE NAME - property 3; it does not matter that the two YThingy columns have different domains.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: are these the same relation - (a) the same four rows listed in a different order, (b) the same rows with columns ordered YThingy, XThingy, ZThingy instead of XThingy, YThingy, ZThingy?
fields.Back:
(a) YES - tuple order has no significance (property 7).
(b) YES - attribute order has no significance (property 5); a tuple is matched to attributes by NAME, not position.

fields.Front: APPLICATION: DEPARTMENT has Location values 'NCB, WSC' and 'BG, NCB'. What is wrong and what is the fix?
fields.Back: The cells are NOT ATOMIC - two values in one cell - violating property 2, so the table is not in first normal form: 'this is not allowed in Ted Codd's version of a relational database'. It is the multi-valued attribute problem from the ER diagram; the fix is a SEPARATE TABLE (mapping rule 6).

fields.Front: APPLICATION: EMPLOYEE(SSN, FirstName, LastName, Department, Position) holds Laura Reid 123, Bob Bryan 005, Sylvia Osborn 125, Bob Bryan 137. Give tuples, attributes, key and a domain - and is two Bob Bryans a problem?
fields.Back: 4 tuples, 5 attributes (degree 5, cardinality 4). Key: SSN, 'because it is used to enforce that each row is unique'. Sample domain: SSN is 000 to 999 (three digits). Two Bob Bryans are NOT a problem - both are from Math and both professors, but their SSNs differ, so the tuples are distinct.

fields.Front: What is a cell, and give the instructor's phone-number example for the 'same domain' property.
fields.Back: A cell is where a row (tuple) and a column (attribute) meet; it may contain only ONE atomic value, 'not ten values separated by commas'. Same domain: if tuple 1 stores a 10-digit phone number, tuple 17 must also store a 10-digit value - 'you can't have one tuple store numbers and another store letters'.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §5.1.2): the book groups the properties of relations under four headings. Name them and the idea each one adds.
fields.Back:
1. ORDERING OF TUPLES: a relation is a SET, so it is not sensitive to tuple order and a shuffled table is the same relation. A FILE, by contrast, has a physical order on disk, and a displayed table has a visual order.
2. ORDERING OF VALUES WITHIN A TUPLE: an ALTERNATIVE DEFINITION makes the schema a set of attributes and each tuple a MAPPING from attributes to values, i.e. a set of (attribute, value) pairs; then attribute order is genuinely irrelevant, and data carried that way is called SELF-DESCRIBING DATA.
3. VALUES AND NULLS: values are ATOMIC, so composite and multivalued attributes are not allowed - the FLAT RELATIONAL MODEL and the FIRST NORMAL FORM ASSUMPTION. Comparing two NULLs is ambiguous (two customers with NULL addresses do not share an address), so avoid NULLs in design.
4. INTERPRETATION OF A RELATION: the schema is an ASSERTION or a PREDICATE and each tuple is a fact satisfying it, under the CLOSED WORLD ASSUMPTION - the only true facts are those in the current state.

fields.Front: Textbook (Elmasri §5.2): what are the three categories of database constraint, and which category do the seven properties of relations belong to?
fields.Back:
1. INHERENT MODEL-BASED or IMPLICIT constraints: built into the data model itself, so a violation cannot even be expressed - 'a relation cannot have duplicate tuples'. THE SEVEN PROPERTIES OF RELATIONS ARE EXACTLY THIS CATEGORY, which is why you cannot 'declare' them.
2. SCHEMA-BASED or EXPLICIT constraints: expressible in the schema through the DDL - domain constraints, key constraints, constraints on NULLs, entity integrity and referential integrity. These are the slides' first two constraint types.
3. APPLICATION-BASED or SEMANTIC constraints, also called BUSINESS RULES: not expressible in the schema, so they must be enforced by application programs, assertions or triggers. These are the slides' semantic integrity constraints.
A fourth family, DATA DEPENDENCIES (functional and multivalued), is used to test the goodness of a design during normalization later in the course.

fields.Text: A relation whose cells each hold exactly one atomic value is {{c1::normalized}}, i.e. in {{c1::First Normal Form (1NF)}}; the convention (though attribute order has no significance) is to put the {{c1::key}} first.

Tuple order has no significance and tuples cannot repeat because a relation is a {{c1::set}}; in practice a query may return {{c1::the same row twice}} and results may be {{c1::sorted}}, but exam answers come from Codd's theory.

Textbook (Elmasri §5.1.2): the no-composite, no-multivalued restriction gives the {{c1::flat relational model}}, and the assumption behind it is called the {{c1::first normal form}} assumption; the book advises that during database design you should {{c1::avoid NULL values as much as possible}}.

Textbook (Elmasri §5.1.2, §9.1.1): the relational model represents facts about entities and facts about relationships {{c1::uniformly, as relations}}, so you have to guess which is which; Chapter 9 therefore names tables made from entities {{c1::entity relations}} and tables made from relationships {{c1::relationship relations}}.
